name: THE PLUM FRY WITH ME BURGER

recipe.history:
The plum — genus Prunus, encompassing dozens of species cultivated across Asia, Europe, and the Americas — is one of the oldest domesticated fruits in human history, with evidence of cultivation in China stretching back over two thousand years. Chinese plum sauce, made from sour plums cooked with vinegar, sugar, and spices, has been a fixture of Chinese cooking for centuries, used as a dipping sauce for roasted meats and as a glaze for duck and pork. Japanese umeboshi — pickled ume plums, sour and intensely flavored — represent a completely different expression of the same fruit, deeply embedded in Japanese food culture as a rice accompaniment and a digestive aid. In European tradition, plum preserves and plum-based sauces are central to the cooking of Eastern Europe, Germany, and the Balkans, where slivovitz (plum brandy) and Powidl (Austrian plum butter) speak to the fruit's centuries-long importance as both food and fermented beverage. The plum's combination of sweetness, acidity, and astringency from its skin makes it one of the most versatile fruits for savory application — it reduces beautifully into a glaze that carries the same fat-cutting brightness as vinegar but with more depth and complexity.

The idea of a fruit-based glaze on a burger patty has its most immediate American precedent in the barbecue tradition, where fruit-enriched sauces — apple, peach, cherry, and plum — have been used as both marinades and finishing glazes throughout the history of American barbecue, particularly in the Carolinas and the Pacific Northwest. The plum glaze on the Plum Fry with Me Burger is applied in the final minute of cooking, when the sugar in the plum reduction caramelizes rapidly against the hot skillet surface, creating a lacquered, slightly sticky exterior on the patty that seals the juices inside while adding a layer of sweet-acid complexity on the outside. Fried shallots — thin-sliced, flour-dredged, fried to a golden crunch — add a contrasting textural register: where the glaze is soft and sticky, the shallots are brittle and savory.

I learned to make plum glaze from a Korean grandmother who lived in my apartment building in my mid-twenties, who made a version of it with Korean plums and gochujang and rice vinegar that she used for braising short ribs. She gave me a jar one Christmas without explanation, and I used it on everything for two weeks — on roast chicken, on pork chops, and eventually on a burger, tentatively at first, and then with increasing conviction as I discovered how naturally plum's sweet-acid depth worked against beef fat. The fried shallots were my addition. She would have put scallions, which would also have been correct, but the fried shallot's crunch seemed to me to be the right structural counterpoint to the glaze's stickiness. I think about that jar of plum glaze every time I make this burger.

The plum glaze on the Plum Fry with Me Burger is applied at the end of cooking, and this creates a specific and non-negotiable requirement: the beef must be at medium rare — 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit — before the glaze goes on. The glaze, which contains sugar, will burn if applied too early to a pan that is still at searing temperature; it must go on in the last thirty to forty-five seconds of cooking over reduced heat, just long enough to lacquer and set but not long enough to char. If the patty is not already at medium rare before the glaze is applied, the cook will be faced with an impossible choice: continue cooking and burn the glaze, or pull early and serve undercooked beef. The only rational solution is to cook correctly to medium rare and then apply the glaze as a finishing gesture. The temperature is not a preference. It is the enabling condition for everything else in the recipe to work.
ingredients: 1 large egg beaten with 1 tbsp water, for egg wash
4 large ripe plums (about 400g), pitted and roughly chopped
6 large shallots, sliced into thin rounds, separated into rings
170g aged Gouda (minimum 12 months) or aged provolone, sliced
fine sea salt and white pepper
softened unsalted butter, for toasting buns
fresh watercress or arugula, for garnish
instructions: 1. Make the buns: Combine flour, yeast, sugar, and salt in the stand mixer bowl with the dough hook. Add warm milk, water, and egg. Mix, then add butter gradually. Knead on medium-high until smooth, 8 minutes. Rise until doubled, 1 to 1.5 hours. Divide into 6 portions (about 140g each), shape, proof 40 minutes. Preheat oven to 375°F (190°C). Egg wash, sesame seeds, bake 18 to 20 minutes. Cool on a rack.

2. Make the plum glaze: Combine chopped plums, balsamic vinegar, red wine, brown sugar, soy sauce, ginger, garlic, black pepper, and allspice in a small saucepan. Bring to a boil, then reduce heat and simmer, stirring occasionally, until the plums have completely broken down and the sauce has reduced to a thick, glossy glaze, about 25 to 30 minutes. Blend with an immersion blender until smooth. Strain through a fine-mesh strainer if desired for a cleaner texture. Season to taste. Keep warm.

3. Make the watercress aioli: Blanch watercress in boiling salted water for 15 seconds, shock in ice water, squeeze dry. Blend blanched watercress, mayonnaise, lemon juice, and garlic in a blender until smooth and pale green. Season with salt and white pepper. Refrigerate.

4. Make the fried shallots: Soak shallot rings in milk for 10 minutes. In a bowl, mix flour, salt, pepper, and cayenne. Drain shallots and dredge in seasoned flour, shaking off excess. Heat 2 inches of neutral oil in a heavy pot to 350°F (175°C). Fry shallots in batches until deep golden and crispy, 2 to 3 minutes. Drain on paper towels, season with salt immediately.

5. Form the patties: Divide beef into 6 portions (about 150g each). Shape into 4-inch patties, 3/4 inch thick, with a center dimple. Season generously with kosher salt and black pepper just before cooking.

6. Cook the patties: Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat until smoking. Cook patties undisturbed for 3 minutes on the first side. Flip and lay aged Gouda slices on each patty. Cook 2 to 2.5 more minutes until the internal temperature reads 130 to 135°F (54 to 57°C) — medium rare. This is the only correct temperature.

7. Reduce heat to medium-low. Spoon 1 to 2 teaspoons of plum glaze over each patty, letting it pool around the cheese. Cook for 30 to 40 seconds only — just long enough for the glaze to lacquer and set, not long enough to burn. Remove patties immediately to a rack and rest 2 to 3 minutes.
8. Toast the buns: Butter the cut sides and toast in the skillet butter-side down over medium heat until golden, about 1 minute.

9. Assemble: Spread watercress aioli on both bun halves. Place fresh watercress or arugula on the bottom bun. Place the glazed, cheese-covered patty on top. Spoon an additional drizzle of plum glaze over the patty. Top with a generous pile of fried shallots. Cap with the top bun and serve immediately.
